Baalpeor
bā´ăl-pē´ôr
n. (the Moabite idol of Mount Peor, and the apostasy of Israel joined to it on the edge of the promised land)
Hebrew baal peor, lord of Peor — the local Baal of the mountain where Balaam had blessed Israel three times. The idol takes its name from the very ground where the curse had failed.

Biblical Definition

“And Israel joined himself unto Baalpeor: and the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel” (Num 25:3), the sin having begun with the daughters of Moab (Num 25:1) and ending in a plague in which “those that died… were twenty and four thousand” (Num 25:9). Moses commanded the judges, “Slay ye every one his men that were joined unto Baalpeor” (Num 25:5), and afterwards reminded the next generation: “all the men that followed Baalpeor, the LORD thy God hath destroyed them from among you” (Deu 4:3). Hosea remembers it as the turning point: “they went to Baalpeor, and separated themselves unto that shame” (Hos 9:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines Baal as an idol among the ancient Chaldeans and Syrians, and notes the word signifies lord, master, or possessor.

expand to see more

BAAL, n. An idol among the ancient Chaldeans and Syrians, representing the sun. The word signifies lord or commander.

IDOLATRY, n. The worship of idols, images, or any thing made by hands, or which is not God.

APOSTASY, n. An abandonment of what one has professed; a total desertion, or departure from one's faith or religion.

Key Scripture

Num 25:1 — "And Israel abode in Shittim, and the people began to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab."

Num 25:3 — "And Israel joined himself unto Baalpeor: and the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel."

Deu 4:3 — "Your eyes have seen what the LORD did because of Baalpeor: for all the men that followed Baalpeor, the LORD thy God hath destroyed them from among you."

Hos 9:10 — "I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness; I saw your fathers as the firstripe in the fig tree at her first time: but they went to Baalpeor, and separated themselves unto that shame; and their abominations were according as they loved."

Modern Corruption

Balaam could not curse Israel with words and destroyed twenty-four thousand of them with a counsel, and Revelation names the tactic by his name.

expand to see more

Numbers 22 through 24 is a comedy of failed cursing: three times Balaam opens his mouth to curse and blessing comes out, and he tells Balak plainly that he cannot go beyond the word of the LORD. Numbers 25 is what happened next, and Numbers 31:16 supplies the missing link — these caused the children of Israel, through the counsel of Balaam, to commit trespass against the LORD in the matter of Peor. What the enemy could not do by opposition he did by invitation. Christ names the doctrine of Balaam to the church at Pergamos in Revelation 2:14 as a live danger to a congregation that had already withstood persecution.

The corruption to name is seduction as the church's chief peril, which the New Testament assumes and modern Christians frequently do not. Congregations brace for hostility and are undone by hospitality; the daughters of Moab invited Israel to sacrifices and the people ate and bowed down. Paul cites this very episode in 1 Corinthians 10:8 as an example written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come, and draws the conclusion in the next verses: wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall. Peor is on the border of Canaan. The failure came within sight of the promise.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew baal (H1168), lord, the Canaanite deity; Peor (H6465), the mountain; tsamad (H6775), to be joined, yoked together.

expand to see more

Hebrew baal (H1168) — Baal, lord, master; Numbers 25:3, Judges 2:13, 1 Kings 18:21.

Hebrew Peor (H6465) — Peor, the mount; Numbers 23:28, 25:18.

Hebrew tsamad (H6775) — to join, be yoked to; Numbers 25:3, 25:5, Psalm 106:28.

Hebrew zanah (H2181) — to commit whoredom; Numbers 25:1, Hosea 4:15.

Hebrew bosheth (H1322) — shame; Hosea 9:10, Jeremiah 3:24.

Usage

"“Israel joined himself unto Baalpeor” — on the edge of the land."

"“All the men that followed Baalpeor, the LORD thy God hath destroyed them.”"

"“They… separated themselves unto that shame” — Hosea's memory of it."
